paras: The attempted lynching of Arthur Robinson took place on the night of April 12, 1903, in Bloomington, Illinois, when a crowd of several hundred people pursued Robinson, a Black depot porter, with threats of lynching after he struck a baseball excursionist on the head. Police reached the barn where he had been cornered and saved him, and he was jailed.

On April 12 about 2,000 people attended a Three-Eye league game in Bloomington between the Joliet and Bloomington teams, 600 of them arriving by special train from Joliet. That night, as the Joliet excursionists waited at the Union Depot for their train, John Hillis of Joliet quarreled with Arthur Robinson, a "negro porter" at the station.

Robinson struck Hillis on the head, with an iron bar according to the press dispatch or with "a heavy shaker from the heating stove" according to the St. Louis Republic. Robinson said that Hillis and a large number of his friends had attacked him and that he acted in self-defense. He fled, and a crowd of several hundred chased him "with the threats of lynching." He was cornered in a barn where he had taken refuge until a squad of police arrived and saved him.

Robinson was jailed to await the outcome of Hillis's case, and Hillis was carried by baggage car to Joliet in serious condition, reported likely to die. No later report of Hillis's condition, a charge against Robinson or action against the crowd was found.

White newspapers carried the episode on April 13, 1903, in two separate versions. A short dispatch ran in the Alexandria Gazette under "Escaped Lynching" and in the Rock Island Argus, which appended it to a baseball column as showing that "baseball enthusiasm is as rampant as ever in that city." The St. Louis Republic's longer special, subheaded "Negro Struck Man on the Head With Iron Shaker," called Hillis "the victim" but gave Robinson's self-defense claim in the most detail. None of the reports named any member of the crowd, and no coverage was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Arthur Robinson
bases: A crowd of several hundred pursued Robinson 'with the threats of lynching' and had him at bay in a barn until police arrived; no one was killed, so this is an attempted lynching (A1, A2).

Robinson was not killed: police reached the barn and saved him (A1, A2). The crowd of several hundred, acting without authority to avenge the blow to Hillis, makes this an attempted lynching rather than a completed one (A1, A2).
The Republic's own special (A1) and the separate press dispatch (A2, reprinted in A3) agree on the blow, the pursuit by several hundred, the police rescue at a barn and the jailing.

accounts.label: Robinson's claim
accounts.gist: Hillis and a large number of his friends attacked him, and he struck Hillis with a shaker from the stove in self-defense.

accounts.label: Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Robinson struck Hillis with an iron bar during an altercation after the ball game; a mob of several hundred pursued him with threats of lynching until police reached the barn.

accounts.label: Republic special
accounts.gist: A controversy at the Union Depot while the 600 Joliet excursionists waited; Robinson fled, was pursued by several hundred threatening vengeance, and was saved by police and jailed.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Republic's headline put the blow first ('Negro Struck Man on the Head With Iron Shaker'), called Hillis 'the victim' and reported Robinson's self-defense claim at length.
The Alexandria Gazette ran the short dispatch under 'Escaped Lynching.'
The Rock Island Argus printed the dispatch at the end of a baseball column as evidence that 'baseball enthusiasm is as rampant as ever' in Bloomington.
